passages.t: ‘My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. To the tune of ‘The Doe of the Dawn.’ A Psalm of David” (verse 1). Then comes the cry: “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me? Why are You so far from saving me, so far from my words of groaning?” (verse 1). “I cry out by day, O my God, but You do not answer, and by night, but I have no rest” (verse 2).

Then he remembers. “Yet You are holy, enthroned on the praises of Israel” (verse 3). “In You our fathers trusted; they trusted and You delivered them” (verse 4).

But his own case seems different. “But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by men and despised by the people” (verse 6). People mock him and shake their heads: “He trusts in the LORD, let the LORD deliver him; let the LORD rescue him, since He delights in him” (verse 8).

So he remembers again, this time his own life. “Yet You brought me forth from the womb” (verse 9). “from my mother's womb You have been my God” (verse 10). He ends this part with a plea: “Be not far from me, for trouble is near and there is no one to help” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
‘The Doe of the Dawn’ is most likely the name of a tune, now lost.

Psalm 22 is a lament that becomes a song of thanks. The first half (verses 1 to 21) is one of the darkest prayers in the Psalms. Notice its rhythm. Complaint, then memory. Worse complaint, then a deeper memory. Each time the trouble grows, the man reaches further back into what he knows of God.

Notice too what he still says. ‘My God.’ He feels abandoned, and he says so. But he says it to God, and he calls him his own. The cry of forsakenness is still a prayer.

‘Enthroned on the praises of Israel’ pictures God seated on his people's songs, as a king sits on a throne. The man stands outside that praise, looking in.

To ‘shake the head’ was a sign of scorn, the way people still roll their eyes or turn away.
passages.later:
Jesus spoke the first line of this psalm as he died on the cross. Mark gives it in Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke, and then translates it: “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (Mark 15:34). Matthew gives “Eli, Eli” (Matthew 27:46), closer to the Hebrew, and records that some bystanders thought he was calling the prophet Elijah (Matthew 27:47).

The Gospels tell the scene in the words of verses 7 and 8. People passed by “shaking their heads” (Mark 15:29). The chief priests said, “He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him” (Matthew 27:43).

Paul explains the darkness of the cross this way: “God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf” (2 Corinthians 5:21).
passages.hard:
Why would Jesus, the Son of God, cry ‘Why have You forsaken Me?’ Did God really abandon him?

The book page on the Psalms sets out the three main ways Christians have read the cry, in its part ‘Why have You forsaken me?’. In short: some stress that by quoting the first line Jesus took up the whole psalm, which ends in trust and praise. Some stress that the cry was real, because he was bearing the sin of others and felt its full weight. Some stress that he took the cry of every forsaken person into his own mouth. Christians often hold these together. They are not enemies.

Jewish readers have long read the psalm in other ways, and those deserve to be known. The Talmud (Megillah 15b) pictures Queen Esther speaking its first line as she went in, uncalled and in danger, to the Persian king. In some Jewish communities the psalm is read at Purim, the feast of Esther. The medieval teacher Rashi read the ‘I’ of the psalm as the people of Israel in exile, crying to God through a long night. These readings and the Christian one share something real: this is the prayer of the righteous sufferer whom God seems to have left.

One thing is plain on every reading. If a man can pray ‘My God, my God, why?’ and still be a man of faith, then so can you.
passages.asks:
Psalm 22 gives you words for the worst moment of faith: when God seems gone. You are allowed to say them. Jesus said them.

It also shows you what to do in that moment. Remember. Remember what God did for others (verse 4). Remember what he has done for you since you were born (verses 9 and 10). The memory does not take the pain away. It gives the pain somewhere to go.

If you feel forsaken right now and the feeling will not lift, please tell someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

passages.t: Bulls, dogs, and ‘they have pierced my hands and feet’
passages.happening:
Now the enemies close in, pictured as animals. “Many bulls surround me; strong bulls of Bashan encircle me” (verse 12). “They open their jaws against me like lions that roar and maul” (verse 13).

His body is failing. “I am poured out like water, and all my bones are disjointed. My heart is like wax; it melts away within me” (verse 14). “My strength is dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue sticks to the roof of my mouth. You lay me in the dust of death” (verse 15).

“For dogs surround me; a band of evil men encircles me; they have pierced my hands and feet” (verse 16). “I can count all my bones; they stare and gloat over me” (verse 17). “They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing” (verse 18).

He prays one last time: “But You, O LORD, be not far off; O my Strength, come quickly to help me” (verse 19). And in the middle of verse 21 the psalm turns: “Save me from the mouth of the lion; at the horns of the wild oxen You have answered me!”
passages.hearers:
Bashan was a high, rich grazing land east of the Sea of Galilee, famous for fat, strong cattle (the prophet Amos calls the rich women of Samaria “you cows of Bashan”, Amos 4:1). Its bulls are power with no pity. The ‘dogs’ are not pets. They were half-wild scavengers that roamed in packs at the edge of towns. The ‘wild oxen’ of verse 21 were huge, horned cattle, now gone from the earth.

The pictures of the body come from the house. Water spilled on the ground cannot be gathered up. Wax melts near a fire. A potsherd is a broken piece of a clay pot, the driest and most useless thing there was.

Dividing a dying man's clothes was a grim, practical custom. Clothes were valuable, and those who had power over him took them.

The turn in verse 21 comes in the middle of a line. He starts by asking to be saved, and ends by saying he has been answered. The psalm never says what happened. It says only that God answered.
passages.later:
All four Gospels tell that the soldiers divided Jesus' clothes (Mark 15:24). John quotes verse 18 in full and explains its two lines: the soldiers divided his outer garments into four parts, and cast lots for his seamless tunic. “This was to fulfill the Scripture: ‘They divided My garments among them, and cast lots for My clothing.’” (John 19:24).

None of the Gospels quotes verse 16. Christians have long read it of the nails of the cross, but the New Testament's use of this psalm does not rest on that verse.
passages.hard:
Does verse 16 really say ‘they have pierced my hands and feet’?

Here the ancient copies differ, and it is honest to say so. The standard Hebrew text, called the Masoretic text, reads a word that means ‘like a lion’: ‘like a lion, my hands and my feet’. Jewish translations follow it, and many Jewish readers say that ‘pierced’ is a Christian reading put onto the Hebrew. They point out that the psalm speaks of lions in verses 13 and 21, and that Isaiah uses the same picture: “Like a lion He breaks all my bones” (Isaiah 38:13).

Other old witnesses have a verb instead. The Greek translation, made by Jewish scholars before the time of Jesus, reads ‘they dug’. A small Psalms fragment from the Judean desert, found at Nahal Hever and copied about the first century AD, has a spelling that many scholars read as a verb, though others say the letter is too faint or the scribe too careless to be sure. Many English Bibles, including the one on this site, read ‘pierced’. Others read differently.

Three things are worth holding. The two readings differ by one small letter, which looks very like another in Hebrew script, so no one needs to accuse the other side of bad faith. The question is still argued by careful scholars on both sides. And the Gospels never quote this verse, so nothing in the Christian reading of Psalm 22 depends on settling it.
passages.asks:
The psalmist does not hide how bad it is. He describes his body, his fear and his enemies in detail. Prayer can be that honest.

Then watch verse 19. With everything closing in, he says, ‘O my Strength.’ When you have nothing left, you can still call God by that name.

passages.t: ‘I will proclaim Your name to my brothers’, and the ends of the earth
passages.happening:
Everything changes. “I will proclaim Your name to my brothers; I will praise You in the assembly” (verse 22). He calls on all Israel to praise God, and gives the reason: “For He has not despised or detested the torment of the afflicted. He has not hidden His face from him, but has attended to his cry for help” (verse 24).

He keeps his promise in public: “I will fulfill my vows before those who fear You” (verse 25). And a feast follows: “The poor will eat and be satisfied” (verse 26).

Then the circle grows. “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the LORD. All the families of the nations will bow down before Him” (verse 27). Even the dying will bow (verse 29). Children not yet born will hear: “They will come and proclaim His righteousness to a people yet unborn” (verse 31). The psalm's last words are “all that He has done.”
passages.hearers:
A person in danger often made a vow: a promise to offer a sacrifice if God rescued him. When the rescue came, he kept the vow at the temple with a peace offering, and the meat was eaten in a shared meal. So ‘the poor will eat and be satisfied’ pictures the rescued man hosting a thanksgiving feast, with the poor as his guests.

Notice how the second half answers the first. He was ‘despised by the people’ (verse 6); now God ‘has not despised’ his torment (verse 24). He cried and had ‘no answer’ (verse 2); now God ‘has attended to his cry’ (verse 24). A psalm that began with his own birth (verses 9 and 10) ends with ‘a people yet unborn’ (verse 31).

The praise moves outward like rings in water: his brothers, Israel, the poor, the whole earth, the dead, the future. One man's rescue becomes the world's song.
passages.later:
Hebrews puts verse 22 in the mouth of the risen Jesus. Because he shared our flesh and our death, “Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers. He says: ‘I will proclaim Your name to My brothers; I will sing Your praises in the assembly.’” (Hebrews 2:11-12). On the morning of his rising, Jesus said to Mary Magdalene, “go and tell My brothers” (John 20:17).

Isaiah shares verse 27's hope: “Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 45:22). Revelation sees it happen: “a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue” (Revelation 7:9).

Jesus' last word in John's Gospel, “It is finished” (John 19:30), has often been set beside the psalm's last line, ‘all that He has done’.
passages.hard:
How can a prayer turn from ‘Why have You forsaken me?’ to a world-wide feast in a few verses? Was the cry not real?

It was real. The turn does not cancel it. The psalm keeps both, side by side, and Christians read both as true of Jesus: the cross and the empty tomb. A reader whose own psalm has not yet turned should notice that the psalmist did not skip the first half to reach the second. Psalm 88 never turns at all, and God kept it in the Bible too.
passages.asks:
When God brings you through something, the psalm asks you to tell it: to ‘my brothers’, in the assembly, at a meal. Rescue is meant to be shared.

And it widens your prayer. Verse 27 asks you to pray for people far beyond your own circle, and for children not yet born, that they will hear ‘all that He has done.’
